item.title: Streaming Protocols Deep Dive: 14 Technologies, Their Limits, and Selection Guide
item.description:
The four codec posts covered how video gets compressed; this one covers how it gets delivered. These 14 streaming technologies don’t operate in the same layer. A complete live streaming pipeline typically follows:

Camera/Encoder → Ingest (RTMP / SRT / RIST / WebRTC-WHIP / WebTransport) → Transcode → Delivery (HLS / LL-HLS / DASH / LL-DASH / HESP / HTTP-FLV) → Viewers

Start by identifying which segment of the pipeline you’re working on, not by asking “which is better.”

item.title: The Surveillance Protocol Panorama: A Four-Layer Map from Access to Compliance — What Each Protocol Is and When to Use It
item.description: The previous post took ONVIF and GB/T 28181 apart down to signaling and messages. But building an NVR means the protocol environment extends well beyond those two: vendor-private APIs on the camera side, a view-library standard on the public-security side, Ministry-of-Transport standards for vehicles, WebRTC for browser viewing, HLS for public distribution, and a national-crypto compliance stack. This post lays out the entire landscape—each protocol gets four sections: what it is → key technical points → its relationship with other protocols → its value to an NVR. Beginners can read it as an index; veterans can jump straight to the priority table.

item.title: MiBeeNvr's Sub-Stream System: No More Lag or Heat on Phone Surveillance
item.description: The two most annoying things about watching surveillance on a phone: it gets hot, and the video stutters. Open four or five tiles on the surveillance grid and every one of them is receiving a high-resolution main stream. The phone decodes and receives at the same time, the battery visibly drains, and the picture keeps hitching. Most people’s first reaction is to replace the phone or switch WiFi to 5 GHz. The bottleneck is not the network; it is the stream being delivered.
